author: A Robot
objectives: Explain apparent retrograde motion (east-to-west reversal) for an outer planet and its periodicity (~every 26 months).
Use heliocentric relative motion to predict why the loop appears without epicycles.
Interpret how changing Earth–planet geometry produces phases: slowdown, stop, reversal (retrograde), and resume eastward drift.
Compare Mars vs. Jupiter and Saturn to justify why the retrograde loop amplitude is smaller for more distant planets.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1 — Watching Mars Loop from Earth
modules.description: Earth-based viewing: students track Mars’s apparent position on a starfield as it slows, stops, reverses, and resumes eastward drift.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define retrograde motion as apparent westward motion against background stars.
Describe the qualitative sequence of the retrograde event (eastward drift → slowdown → stop → westward loop → resume eastward).
Separate apparent sky motion from real changes in Mars’s orbit.
instructions: Track the Mars marker as it moves across the starfield.
Use the labels to note the current stage of the retrograde event.

clips.changeMeaning: Sets an initial reference point on the starfield and establishes the baseline stage where Mars drifts eastward relative to background stars.
clips.narration: Imagine observing Mars night after night. Against the fixed background stars, Mars doesn’t move smoothly forever—it slows, stops, reverses, and then resumes its usual eastward drift. That apparent reversal is called retrograde motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the Mars marker to a nearby eastward position and updates labels to link slowdown to reduced apparent angular motion.
clips.narration: First, the eastward motion slows. In the sky, that means the step between successive positions gets smaller—as Mars approaches a turning point.

clips.changeMeaning: Places the marker at the loop ‘top’ where apparent speed is minimal, then updates direction to indicate the start of retrograde.
clips.narration: Mars reaches a point where its apparent motion nearly stops, then reverses into westward motion—tracing the loop across the constellations.

clips.changeMeaning: Advances the marker along the westward arc to represent most of the retrograde loop while emphasizing that this is apparent, not orbital, reversal.
clips.narration: Over the next weeks, Mars moves westward relative to the stars. After about two months, the westward motion ends and Mars resumes its eastward path.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the marker back to an eastward-drifting position and adds the periodicity (~26 months) to connect this event to a repeating observational pattern.
clips.narration: Finally, Mars slows again and resumes its normal eastward drift. The overall pattern repeats about every 26 months.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2 — Explaining Retrograde with Heliocentric Relative Motion
modules.description: Heliocentric view: Earth moves faster on its inner orbit and overtakes Mars, producing the apparent sky loop phases.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Model how Earth’s faster inner orbital speed leads to ‘overtaking’ geometries.
Link the moment of strongest retrograde to the changing line-of-sight projection.
Use the sequence of phases (behind → approach → overtaking → after pass) to predict apparent motion direction.
instructions: Watch how Earth (blue) and Mars (red) move relative to the Sun.
Follow the phase label to connect the orbital geometry to the apparent sky motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Initial placement sets a ‘behind’ configuration. The phase label connects this geometry to the typical eastward apparent drift.
clips.narration: In the heliocentric picture, Earth orbits closer to the Sun, so Earth moves faster. When Earth is behind Mars along their respective orbits, Mars appears to drift eastward.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves Earth forward around its inner orbit while Mars advances more slowly on its outer orbit, representing the slowing phase.
clips.narration: As Earth moves forward, it approaches Mars’s orbital region. The relative motion along the line of sight shrinks, so Mars’s apparent eastward drift slows down.

clips.changeMeaning: Positions correspond to Earth being ‘ahead’ in the relevant projection. The phase text highlights the reversal (retrograde) outcome.
clips.narration: During overtaking, Earth reaches a geometry that flips the sign of the projected relative motion. That’s when retrograde is strongest—Mars appears to move westward against the background stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth is moved beyond the overtaking configuration, and the label indicates the return to eastward apparent motion as the retrograde loop completes.
clips.narration: After Earth passes, the relative motion again favors eastward apparent movement. The loop closes and Mars resumes its normal drift.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3 — Comparing Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn Retrograde
modules.description: Compare apparent retrograde loop strength for Mars vs. Jupiter and Saturn using the same relative-motion logic.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare loop amplitudes qualitatively across multiple planets.
Explain why more distant planets loop less dramatically: smaller relative angular-speed effect.
Translate the comparison back to observational behavior near oppositions.
instructions: Mentally compare the maximum westward displacement for each planet marker.
Then identify which planet shows the strongest retrograde loop and why.

components.text: Top: Mars • Middle: Jupiter • Bottom: Saturn

clips.changeMeaning: Starts all three markers aligned in an initial eastward-drift configuration so students can compare how far each reverses later.
clips.narration: All three planets loop, but Mars makes the biggest one. Jupiter and Saturn are farther from the Sun, so their orbital speeds differ less from Earth’s faster inner orbit.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the Mars marker much closer to its turning region while Jupiter and Saturn shift less, visually reinforcing reduced retrograde amplitude.
clips.narration: As Earth begins overtaking, Mars’s apparent motion slows and the loop grows. Jupiter and Saturn also slow, but their direction change is smaller because the relative-motion effect is reduced.

clips.changeMeaning: Places Mars far to the east-to-west side relative to its start (large westward displacement) while Jupiter/Saturn remain near their original tracks (small displacement).
clips.narration: During the retrograde interval, Mars reverses more noticeably—tracing a prominent westward arc. Jupiter and Saturn reverse slightly, producing smaller, flatter loops.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves all planets back to an eastward-drift configuration and preserves Mars’s larger net displacement, completing the comparative narrative.
clips.narration: After Earth passes, all three markers resume eastward motion—but Mars still shows the most dramatic overall loop. The key idea is relative motion, not changing planetary orbits.
